exercise1.hint: Parse first, then take the minimum, then format it back. On ISO-formatted text the alphabetical answer happens to agree, which is exactly why the habit matters when the format changes.

exercise2.prompt: Parsing Dates: How many dates are usable

hiddenCases.name: a clean column has nothing unusable
a column of junk parses nothing
the two always total the column length
the right tool does the work

exercise2.hint: to_datetime with errors="coerce" turns the failures into NaT instead of raising. notna() counts the good ones and isna() the bad.

questions.prompt: A date column read from a CSV is what, until you convert it?
questions.explain: And text sorts alphabetically, so "02/2024" comes before "1/2023".

questions.prompt: What does errors="coerce" do to an unparseable date?
questions.explain: NaT is the datetime equivalent of NaN, and counting them tells you how bad the column is.

questions.prompt: A British file writes 03/04/2024 for 3 April. What do you need?
questions.explain: Both readings succeed, so nothing warns you — every date whose day is 12 or under is silently wrong.

questions.prompt: Which is cheaper than converting after the load?
questions.explain: And it means the column is never text long enough for you to sort it by accident.
